description: Regularize the search toward tiny rule descriptions, tiny interface alphabets, and tiny slope sets, then see which compact motifs still survive exact extraction. This treats compactness as an engineering bias for discovering reusable modules rather than as a theorem about arithmetic Kakeya itself.
mathematical_formalization: Minimize a description-length objective DL = DL(\rho)+DL(X)+DL(\mathcal{I}) subject to S_{\mathrm{extract}}(\rho,X,\mathcal{I}) \le \tau. Search the Pareto frontier between extracted score, rule-table size, and interface complexity.
analogical_connections: muNCA-style compression is repurposed from texture synthesis to certificate motif discovery.
Minimal rule tables act like compressed proof macros.
Description length provides a bias toward motifs that may transfer across scales and search regimes.
implementation_hypothesis: Search discrete rule families with explicit compression penalties: truth-table sparsity, few active channels, and small X. Retain a motif only if a tiny rule still yields an exact low-score certificate after compilation.
experiment_seed: Run a Pareto search over rule families on 4x4 and 5x5 grids, using exact extraction for every nondominated candidate. Compare compressed-search winners to unregularized winners to see whether compactness helps or merely hurts score.

novelty_claim: The bridge is new only if description-length pressure helps discover exact arithmetic certificates that would be hard to find by unconstrained search.
differentiation: This is not texture compression and not just small-model enthusiasm. Compactness is valuable here only as a search prior for exact witness structures.
